Why does the air in a large city stay several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside on a clear, calm night, and what single mechanism best explains why that night-time gap is larger in some cities than in others?

accepted.claim: On a clear, calm night the city remains warmer because concrete and asphalt store daytime sensible heat and release it slowly after sunset; the cross-city magnitude of this nocturnal warm anomaly depends mainly on sky view factor, because deep street canyons with low sky view trap longwave radiation and suppress radiative cooling, making the night-time gap larger in denser, taller cities.

The night-time urban heat island is primarily an evapotranspiration deficit: impervious urban surfaces lack vegetation and soil moisture, so daytime sensible heat storage is not dissipated as latent heat, leaving more heat to be released nocturnally; the gap is larger in cities with less irrigation and green space.

The dominant cross-city modulator of nocturnal UHI is anthropogenic heat flux from vehicles, buildings, and industry; cities with higher nighttime energy use and population density release more sensible heat directly into the urban boundary layer, maintaining a larger temperature gap.

The nocturnal UHI gap is best explained by differential longwave radiative cooling driven by emissivity and surface properties: urban materials have different emissivity and thermal admittance than natural surfaces, causing cities to cool more slowly after sunset, and the gap scales with impervious surface fraction.

The single best cross-city modulator is the sky view factor (SVF), which directly determines how much outgoing longwave escapes to the cold sky sink versus being intercepted and re-emitted by building walls; cities with lower SVF have a larger nocturnal gap.

The nocturnal UHI gap is primarily driven by anthropogenic heat flux: vehicles, buildings, and industry inject sensible heat into the urban atmosphere day and night. On a clear, calm night with low wind, this heat is not advected away, so it accumulates and keeps the city warmer. The single best cross-city modulator is population density (or energy consumption): cities with higher anthropogenic heat emissions have a larger nocturnal gap.

The nocturnal UHI is a coupled storage-and-trapping phenomenon, but the single best cross-city modulator is the ratio of urban impervious surface fraction to sky view factor (ISF / SVF), which captures both how much daytime heat is stored and how slowly it is released at night. Cities with high impervious cover and low sky view have the largest nocturnal gaps; cities with either low impervious cover or high sky view have smaller gaps.

The single best cross-city modulator is the urban soil moisture deficit, which is greatest in cities with extensive impervious cover and low irrigation, making the nocturnal gap larger in more impervious and drier cities.
